blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: State the consequences of a price change for the new equilibrium price and the quantity sold in each direction a curve can shift, read those consequences from a demand-and-supply diagram described in words, and name the parties they land on.

blocks.heading: Four shifts, four consequences
blocks.text: The consequences of a price change are read as a pair: the new equilibrium price, and the new equilibrium quantity - the quantity bought and sold at that price over a period, the market's sales. Where demand shifts right and supply holds, both tend to rise: consumers pay more and sellers sell more. Where demand shifts left, both tend to fall. Where supply shifts right, the price tends to fall while sales tend to rise; where supply shifts left, the price tends to rise while sales tend to fall.

blocks.heading: A bumper harvest at Gobabis
blocks.text: Good rains swell the cabbage harvest around Gobabis: the supply curve shifts right, and at the old price of N$15 a head there are more cabbages than buyers take. The price falls to N$10 a head, and sales rise from 400 to 520 heads a week, since 520 - 400 = 120 heads. Households pay less for each head, and traders usually sell more heads at the lower price. Rice traders near Can Tho in Vietnam see the same after a strong Mekong harvest.

blocks.heading: When demand falls
blocks.text: A decrease in demand works the other way. Suppose a mine near Rosh Pinah lays off a third of its workers. Incomes in the town fall, and incomes are a condition of demand, so the demand curve for takeaway meals shifts left from D1 to D2 while supply stays where it was. At the old price of N$50 a meal, sellers now offer more meals than buyers take: a surplus. Sellers cut the price to clear unsold food, and the market moves down the unchanged supply curve to a new equilibrium at N$42, with sales down from 900 to 700 meals a week, since 900 - 700 = 200. Both the equilibrium price and the quantity sold have fallen. Households that still buy pay less per meal, while the takeaway owners sell fewer meals at a lower price, so their takings fall from 900 x N$50 = N$45 000 to 700 x N$42 = N$29 400 a week.

blocks.heading: Reading the consequence off the diagram
blocks.text: A demand-and-supply diagram shows the story in words. Put the price of the good on the vertical axis and the quantity on the horizontal axis. Draw and label the original demand curve D1 and supply curve S1, crossing at the original equilibrium. When a market condition changes, shift the curve whose condition moved, in the correct direction, and hold the other still. The new crossing, marked and labelled, is the new equilibrium: read off the new price and the quantity sold, and state in words what the diagram shows - which way the price and the sales moved, and on whom it landed.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: How strongly sales respond to a new price is measured in topics 2.7 and 2.8; the equilibrium the shifts settle at is topic 2.5's.
